entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -7'/ie sina of the sect and the ,iM of the tri"be. "For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision," etc. In the preceding verses Paul stated one purpose for which he left Titus in Crete, viz. to set in order "the things that are wanting," and to ordain elders in every city. He recognized ai once, not only the importance of order in the new community, but also the importance of appointing men who, intellectually and morally, were qualified for its establishment and continuance. In these verses he gives Titus directions .as to his aggressive work in Crete. He was to do battle with sin. "For there are many unruly [menJand vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision: whose mouthA mnst be stopped, who subvert [overthrowJwhole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake." The great work of the gospel minuter iB to do baetle wi,th ,in. In the text, sin is referred to a.s appearing in two aspects, in religiom sect and in national character. L ill BELIGIOUB BEOT. "Specially they of the circumcision." These, undoubtedly, are Judaizing Christians, men who pretended to be converted to Christianity, men who sought not only to mingle Judaic elements with the new religion, but to inculcate and disseminate it in that form. Observe the desoription of sin as it appeared in this religious sect--these men of the circumcision. Here is: 1. Factiousness. "Un~uly." Nat onlv would thev not bow to the established order of the Church, but not to the OH, I, 1-16.] THE EPISTLE TO 'l'J'l'li::S. cl spirit and principles of the new religion, They would not yield to the masterhood of Christ, the Author and Substance ofthe gospel; they were self-willed. They would have o. sect of their own. 2. 0stentatioo. "Vo.in talkers." Vo.in, not merely in the sense of proud, but in the sense of emptiness. In truth, a.ea rule, the emptiest men, intellectually, are at once the most conceited and loquacious. They talk, not for the edification of others, but for the gratification of themselves. Their fluency, whilst it wins the admiration of fools, deludes the ignorant, and disgusts the thoughtful. 3. Falsehood. "Deceivers." All merely nominal Christians are deceivers. They practically misrepresent the doctrines they profess to hold. 4. Mi11'4ievousness. "Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert roverthrow] whole houses." "The translation should IUD, 'seeing they Rubvert,' etc. There was, indeed, grave cause why these men should be put to silence: the mischief they were doing in Crete to the Christian cause was incalculable. It was no longer individuals that their poisonous teaching a.ffected, but they were undermining the faith of whole families. For an example bow Titus and his presbyters were to stop the mouths of these teachers of what was false, comp. Matt. xxii. 34-46, where the Lord, by his wise, powerful, yet gentle words, first put the Sadducees to silence, and then so o.nswE!red the Pharisees 'that neither durst any man from that day ask him any more questions'" (Dr. Ellicott). 5. Greed. "Teachin~ things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.'' All the speeches they made, all the influence they exerted, sprang from sordid motives. Sin bas a thousand branches and but one root, and that root is selfishness. How many, in what we call the religiou, world, are found teaching things which they ought not, for "filthy lucre's sake"- things that gratify popular taste, that agree with popular prejudice, chime in with the popular thought! All this to fill their pews and to enrich their coffers. Now, these sins which are discovered in the religious sect are prevalent outside of all religions ; but they receive a peculiar colour, shllf"I, enormity, and mischievousness when we find them in the religious realm. The de",i is less hideous amongst his fellows in hell than be is amongst the sons of God. Hence, to do battle with sin in these religious forms is the grand work of a true preacher; and truly, in this age, and here in England, he will find these sins on every band. He will see /actiousne:;s building up sects, and little sects within sects; ostentation-vain speakiug, bmggardism, sometimes cooing a.nd sometimes bawling, everywhere; falsehood-rogues rubing themselves in the ~arb of sainthood, wolves in sheep's clothing; mischievou.sness-by their empty words and pernicious example subverting "whole houses," filling the domestic air with poisonous cant; greed-the gospel itself made a trade, and vested interests created in connection with doctrines and doings antagonistic to the life and spirit of him whom they call ~faster. Ah me I conventional religion is a calumny on the religion of Christ. Never was a Luther wanted in Christendom more than now. He is wanted to substitute the pure gospel of Christ for the denominationo.lized gospel. II. IN NATIONAL CHARAarEB. "One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said, The Cretans are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies [idle gluttons]." There are three sins mentioned here which seem to have prevailed amongst the Cretans as a race. 1. Lying. " The Cretans are alway liars." Who made this charge against the Cretans? Paul says," One of themselves, even a prophet of their own." The quotation is from a poem on 'Oracles,' by Epimenides, of Pbrestus, who flourished e.c. 600, lived to the age of a hundred and fifty, and was supposed to have been a sleeper in a cave for fifty-seven years. He appears to have deserved the title prophet in the fullest sense. Plato speaks of him as a Divine man. The Cretans were characterized by the sin of lying-" alway liars." This expression was quoted by Callimachus in his •Hymn to Zeus,' and well known in antiquity. "The very word 'to Cretize' (Kretizein), or to play the part of a Cretan, was invented as a word synonymous with 'to deceive,' 'to utter a lie;' just as Oorinthiazein, 'to play the po.rt ofa Corinthian,' signified 'to commit a still darker moral offence.' Some writers su~gest that this despicable vice of lying was received as a bequest from the early Phren1cian colonists." 2. Sensuality. "Evil beasts." Not only liars, but gross and sensual, living in animalism and for it. All m11n may be called "beasts" who attend to their animal appetites a.e means of gratification rather than of relief. He who seeks happiness from his senses rather than from bis soul is a beast; he who seeks it from without rather than from within is not better than a beast. The happiness of a true man cannot stream into him from without; it 22 THE EPISTLE 'l'O TITUS. [OB. I. 1-16. mUBt well up from the depths of hie own high thinkings 1md pure affections. Gluttony. "Slow bellies [idle gluttons]." .Their f!lu~tony ~ade them dull, heavy, and indolent. Such are what may be called tnbal or national sms. They were not confined to the Cretans, but for them the Cretans were notorious. These aM national. But are 1h~se sins extinct in England? Ba,·e we no lying here? Our social air is impregnated with falsehood. Ha"e we no sensuality and gluttony? Yes, alas! tens of thousands are every day pampering themselves with luxuries, whilst millions are being starved to death. Here, thtJn, are common sins with which the preacher has to do battle. He ha.s to "rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith." CoNCLus10N. A true preacher, then, has no easy task. He ha.s to wage fierce battle with the sins that are around him-the sins of the sect and tile sins of the tribe. He is not to pander to men's tastes, nor to battle with mere opinions and theories, but with si,u; ; be must "resist unto blood, striving against sin." " For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil."-D. T.

entries.title: TIT 1:15
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -The supreme importance of moral character. "Untv the pure all things a:e pure: but unto them that are deiled and unbelieving is nothing pure," etc. We notice, at the outset, two facts suggested by the pa.ssage. 1. That there is an essential diiferenre in the moral characters ofmen. There are some "pure" and some' "defiled," some holy and some unholy. What is the underlying inspiring principle that makes this difference? The predominant dispo~ition. Perhaps there is no moral being in the universewho is not under the masterhood of some one sentiment or passion, to which can be traced, as to a mainspring, all the motions of his being. This controlling tendency is the moral monarch of souls, or, in Scripture language, is the moral "heart of the man." This supreme disposition exists in all men in two distinct and opposite forms, either in sympathy with the true, the right, and the spiritual, or in sympathy with the false, the wrong, and the material. That soul alone is pure whose governing sympathy is God and the true. Supreme love for the supremely good is the true life of the soul, and the fountain of all its virtues. He whose controlling sympathies run not thus, is impure and corrupt. 2. That the outward world is to men acoording to this difference. The whole external universe is to a man according to the moral state of his soul. " As a man thin.keth in his heart, so is he "-so is he in relation to himself, to all without, and to God. This being so, the text teaches the supreme importanre of moral character. Let us look at- L THE MORALLY PURE IN RELATION TO ALL THINGS. "Unto the pure all things are pure." This is true in relation to three things. 1. In relation to appearanre. The proverb goes that the greatest rogues are ever the most suspicious. A thoroughly selfish, ungodly soul will see but little good even in the best men. It is a law that man judges his fellow by himself, and the more corrupt a man is, the more severe his judgment on 01hers. A good man is neither given to sUBpicion nor censoriousness; he sees some good in all men. 2. In relation to influenre. The influence of all outward things upon men is dependent on their moral character. Our Lord says, "Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man, but that which cometh out of the mouth defileth a man." The moral character is an all-traneformative power in the centre of ma11's being. It turns the unclean into the clean, and the reverse. A good man, like the bee, can extract honey from the bitterest plant; or, like the lEolia.n harp, can turn the shrieking wind into mUBic. 3. In relation to appropriation. As the body lives by appropriating the outward, so does the soul; and as the effects i,f the appropriation, whether universal or otherwise, depend on the condition of the body's health, as the appropriation of a diseased body only increases the physical ailment; so with the soul. A corrupt soul appropriates, even from the most strengthe11ing and refreshing menns of spiritual improvement, that which weakens and destroys. Pharaoh and hie host got moral mischief out of the ministry of Moses; and the men of Capernaum were µressed into a deeper and darker hell through the elevating and e111ightening ministry of Jesus of Nazareth. Mark, then, the supreme importance of moral character. ll. THE MORALLY DEFILED IN &ELATION TO ALL THINGS. "Unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is r,othing pure; but even their mind and conscience is de~led." Bere is the converse.. Ma~k, in ?a-sin_!/:, t\:rec thingR. 1. The srhere ofthe def!le:,nent. "The mind and conscience.' "'l he 11,UJ<l, says a modern expositor, "1s the wilhng as OR, I, 1-16.) THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. 23 well as the thinking part of man, ae it hae been well defined the human spirit (pnewna) in one of its aspects, not simply qU4lenua cogitat, et intelligit, but a!BO quater,us vu.lt. Defilement of this mind (now) means that the thoughts, wishes, purposes, activities, are all stained and debaeed. The eecond of these, the conscience (BUneidesis), ie the moral consciousness within, and that which is ever bringing up the memory of the past, with its omissions and commissions, its errors, its cruel, heartless unkindness, its eelfish disregard of others. When this ie defiled, then this last safeguard of the soul is hroken down. The man and woman of the defiled conscience is self-satisfied, hard, impenitent to the last. Every part and faculty of the soul is stained with sin. The body may be cleansed by ceremonial ablutions, and the external manners and speech kept pure by culture and civilization, but the soul be black ; the outside of the "cup and of the platter clean," but inside full of corruption. 2. The cauae of the defilement. "They profess that they know God, but in works they deny him." There is nothing, perhaps, so morally defiling to the soul as religious hypocrisy. The man who with the lip professes to know God, and who in the life denies him, gets deeper stains upon his soul than the agnostic who professes that he knows nothing about him. What million., in our churches every Sunday publicly, at each service, a.vow with their lip their belier' in God, but in their week-day life "he is not in all their thoughts"! Thus souls get deeply dyed in corruption in Christian churches. 3. The hideousness of the defilemimt. "Being abominable e.nd disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate." However fair their conduct in the religious observances, they are "abominable" within, hideous to the eye of God. However rigorous in their observances and religious ordinances, they are "disobedient" in heart, they outrage moral laws; however useful they regard themselves and apµear to others, they are "reprobate," they are rejected and worthless. These "defiled" in soul defile everything without ; all outward things in their appearance, influences, and appropriation are to them corrupt. CoNcLUSION. Mark : 1. The natwral soveTeignty of the human soul. We are not necessarily the creatures of the outward; we have within the power to bend circumstances to our will, to get good out of evil, to turn outward dissonance into music, deformity into beauty, poison into nourishment. Let us adore our Maker for this wonderful endowment-an endowment which guards us from the coercion of outward forces, secures to us an inward freedom of action, and enables us to put all outward things in subjection to our own spiritual selves. 2. The depend,ency ofthe soul's destiny 1m itself. A man's destiny depends upon his moral character, and his character depend,; upon himself. As food, however nutritious, cannot ad!:nioister strength to a man's body without the digestive and appropriative power, so no external influences, however good and useful in themselves, can raise a man's soul without the right actionof its faculties. Man cannot be made good. His body may be borne to the summit of a lofty mountaio without the use of his limbs, but if his soul is to ascend "the holy hill of the Lord," he must climb it every inch himself. Fortune or patronage may raise him to some eminent social position, but he cannot reach a single stage of moral dignity-the true dignity of man-apart from hi~ own earnest endeavours. The transformative power of the soul is to external circumstances what the builder is to the materials out of which he rears his edifice. The choicest materials may be brought together-gold, marble, and cedar-but unless the builder use them with artistic skill they will never take the form of a beautiful structure. entries.content: -Prcutic.al godliness the end of spirit'U,(],l doctrfM. Paul soars very high in reijpect of the hidden things oi' God.. 'l'o were given more abundant revelations of heavenly mysteries. The teaching of St. none of the apostles Caught up into the OR, D. 1-16,) THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. l9 third heaven, hearing unspeakable words, saturated with gifts of the Holy Ghost, he was able to lead men's souls ink> depths and heights of unseen things as no other tl.'acher was. Hi~ eloquent tongue, pouring forth the riches of knowledge of an enlightened heart, could speak of God's love to man, of hie eternal purposes, of bis predestinating grace, of the coming and kingdom of the Lord Jesus, of the resurrection of the dend, of the inheritance of the saints in light, in words of wisdom and power certainly not inferior oo those of the very chiefest apostles of Christ. And yet, in dealing with the practical duties of Ohristian men and women, and in teachin11: morality as an essential part of Christianity, there is a particularity of detail, a searching application of truth, an earnest tone of warning and of exhortation, which could not be nceeded by any teacher of ethics who knew of nothing else bat human condnct and the present interests of society. With St. Paul, familiarity with the highest doctrines of revelation does not depreciate the importance of the humblest duties of daily life; it rather magnifies it, and raises those duties from an earthly to a heavenly platform. If St. Paul's sole end and aim in his apostolic labours bad been to bring the daily !ifs of every class of the community to whom he wrote into accordance with the law of righteousness, and to make human life on earth pure and happy, he could not have dwelt upon those details of practice, on which the economy or society depends for its comfort and happiness, with more earnestness and particularity than he has done. The demeanour of old men, the behaviour of old women, the influence·of the aged upon the young, the innermost domestic duties of the wife and the mother, words, deeds, looks, dress, temper, disposition, affections, all comes under the constraining influence of the gospel as preached by St. Paul. In like manner that degraded portion of mankind whose condition was so pitiable in the Roman empire, the slaves, of whom there were such numbers in every considerable household, is brought under the elevating influence of Christian motive. Relations and duties full of nought but pain and humiliation in themselves, and leading naturally to the vices which are born of degradation, are elevated at once into platforms of eminent virtue. Under the holy influences of Chr,istian faith new principles are called into life, new motives of thought and action a.re a.wakeue:l, and the low life of the dishonest, insolent, and deceitful slave becomes the arena for the exercise of some of the highest virtues of the saint. What a lesson we have here for the Christian teacher! If the parish priest, whose intercourse with his flock brings him into contact with the infirmities and sins of the various classes of his parishioners, would bend his strength in this direction, and upon the basis of the doctrine of grace would builrl the superstructure of a severe and minute instruction in the details of a really holy life, the value of a parochial ministry would be seen to the full. Christianity in the family, Christianity in the shop, Uhristianity in the daily intercourse of map with man, would be a preaching of Christ to the world which would put the caviller to shame, and which no adversaries would be ahle to gainsay or to resist.

There is to be a healthy action of these graces in old age. As if in coutrast with the diseases, weakness, and age of the btody. The aged have seen their best days, and they ouoht to reconcile the decay of nature with the increase o{ grace, so as to make human lif; to its extreme limit resplendent with beauty and truth. 2. entries.content: -The duties ofaged women and yown,g women. As woman had attained through Christianity a position of equality beside man, it was necessary to remind her that her new position involved serious responsibilities. I. THE DUTIES OF AGED WOMEN. 1. In demeanour as becometh holinu,, (1) There is an appeal to their own judgment as to what is decorous and beautiful in the Christian character. They had an experimental knowledge of the gospel, and they understood the nature and extent of its obligations as affecting their sex. (2) There was to be a harmony between their position and their character as godly women- " women professing godliness" (1 Tim. ii. 10). Their holy calling should manifest itself in their deportment, dress, speech, silence, and, above all, "in a meek and quiet spirit." 2. Not slanderer,. (1) Old age has no active employment, but it has an active memory and a hi1sy tongue. Thus there is a temritation for the old, unleBB the grace of God has give11 the tongue of kindness, to become censorious, malignant, and bitter, avengin;:?; themselves the more with their tongues for their very incapacity to avenge themselves in other ways. (2) There is nothing more beautiful or saintly in this world than a true mother in Israel, the presiding genius of her family circle, speaking the words or charity, softness, and kindness to all within her reach. (3) It would be an utter travesty of the gospel for aged Christian women to he slanderers, because they would thus (a) separate friends (Prov. xvi. 28); (b) inflict deadly wounds in character (Prov. xviii. 18); (c) bring dishonour on the gospel; (d) and cause discords iu the Church. 3. (2) It WB!l a moderate demand that they should give up the 6lavish addictedness to wine so common in Crete. She who follows the habit is a slave, and would soon lose the Bense of her degradation. The early converts would, perhap~, plead the privileges of their age and country, and use wine ll.H a solace in old age; but Titus is to teach them that hoary ha.ire give no OR, D, 1-16.] THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. 81 liberty to BUch a habit. (3) We see bow the gospel purifies the habits and usages of social life. 4. Teacher, of good things. (1) The apostle thus prescribes the right use of the tongue to those who were to be "no slanderers." (2) Their teaching wail not to be in public addresses, which were forbidden (1 Tim. ii. 12), but in private life. (3) The substance of their teaching was not to be" old wives' fables," not superstitious ceremonies, or things of evil report, but things sound, pure, and honest. II. TRE DUTIES OF YOUNG WOMEN. They are regarded as under the instruction anrl guidance of the aged women. In Ephesus, Timothy was exhorted to teach the younger women, but it is probable that the state of the Cretan community required that the instructions of Titus should be supplemented by the more practical and continuous guiC:ance of the elderly women. The young women were to be schooled to their duties in a wise manner. 1. They were to be lovers of their hus"bands. (1) The wife would find in tLis love the source of her strength, the husband the solace for his cares, and the children the guarantee for their happiness and welfare. (2) A loving wife is .(a) a blessing to her husband (Prov. xii. 4); (b) brings him honour (Prov. xxxi. 23); (c) secures his confidence (Prov. xxxi. 11); (d) earns his praises (Prov. xxxi. 28). 2. Lovers of their children. (1) The love of a. mother may be instiuctive, but religious fanaticism and brutal separation can make her more unfeeling than the brutes. Rousseau would not keep bis children in his house, but sent them to a public hospital ; a sign, said Burke, that "bears love their young and lick them into shape, but bears are not philosophers." In India. infants a.re often destroyed by a mother's hands, nnder the influence of religious delusion. (2) The first duty of a. Christian woman is to make her home happy, which is impossible except on a. basis of love to husband and children. (3) Religion revives natural affection as it revives all the weakened faculties of our nature, and gives it new power for good. The religious training of the young is impossible without t.be experience of a mother's love. 3 Discreet. Young women, in a new position or Christian privilege, might be tempted to rashness, enthusiasm, and impulsive conduct. 1'hey were to be wise and careful in their conduct both at home and abroad. 4. Chaste. In act, speech, thought, and dress, finding their true happiness in their husband's society. There are many high motives for a pure womanhood (1 Cor. vi. 19; 1 These. iv. 7). 5. Workers at home. (1) The wife's business is in her household, not in the great world of society. Religion gains no honour when home duties are neglected. (2) Her husband's interests a.re preserved by her industry at home. (3) Gadding abroad and busying one's self in other people's affairs tends to the spreading of evil. 6. Good. Such women are to be kindly and thoughtful in their family relationships, especially to servants, and not niggardly or exacting. "Their thriftiness must not degenerate into avarice." 7. Obedient to their OW1I husbands. (1) This is their great duty, and thus they become types of the Church's submission to Christ. (2) Obedience would recommend the gospel to unbelieving husbands, for attention to this precept would prevent "the Word of God from being blasphemed." Grace does not deliver us frow the obligations of nature (1 Cor. vii. 4-16).-T. C.

entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -The grace of God the true ground of all samtification. Th1, apostle now sete forth the real foundation on which thie exhortation to practical dnty on the part of eervante, and, inueed, of people of every age and sex, is baeed. I. THE GRACE OJ" Goo. "For the grace of God that bringeth salvation t.o all men hath appeared." 1. This grace isfrom God, as it., eternal Fountain,from which it flows to men. (1) He was not made gracious by the work of the Son, for he was the God of grace from the beginning. The work of the Son only manifested it (John iii. 16). (2) The grace is from the Son as well as the Father. Grace is in every conceivable way connected with the Person of the Mediator in Scriptnre (1 Cor. xvi. 23; Gal. i. 6; 1 Thess. v. 28). The Father and the Son are one in the rreeness or their love to mankind. (3) Grace is also connected with the Holy Ghost, who is called ,. the Spirit of grace" (Heh. x. 29), because be applies it and seals us to the day of redemption. Thus ~race bas its origin in the Father, its manifestation in the Son, ite end in the Holy Ghost. 2. The nature of this grace. (1) It is the free gift of God to mankind in the gospel of Christ. It is thus opposed to the idea of merit in man. Works, therefore, do not procure our salvation. (~) The grace must necessarily be worthy cf the character of God. (a) The gift is worthy, for it ie his own Son. (b) The end is worthy, for it is his own glory and man's salvation. (c) The instrumental conditiou is worthy, for it is faith. 3. The scope of this grace. "That bringetb salvation to all men." (1) It ie the only thing that can bring salvation to mnn. He cannot be saved by worke, nor by philosophy, nor by man. (2) It has a wide scope. It "bringeth salvation to all men." (a) This does not imply that all men will eventually be saved, for Scripture expressly asserts the very contrary. (b) The connection of the passage explains the universality of the reference: "Servants, be obedient to your masters, that you may adorn the doctrine of God your Saviour; for bis grace is for slave and master alike." There is no respect ot persons with him. (c) It signifies that grace is the only means by which salvation is possible for the racP of man. 4. The manifestation ofgrace. (1) la the Incarnation. (2) In the work of Christ. (3) In the energy of the Holy Spirit. "The darkness is past; the true light now shineth" (1 John ii. 8). II. THE EFFECTS OF THE GRACE OF Goo. "Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should "live soberly, righteously;and godly in this present world." 1. This grace first manifests itself by teaching, just as the first thing in creation was light. It must begin with teaching, and the Spirit of God is given "to teach us all things" (John xiv. 26). The original word implies the idea of a dieciplining process, Affected by the grace of God to correct the inherent naughtiness of the heart. 2. The grace of God works toward the rejection of evil, for it teaches us" to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts." (1) Tho denial is in heart and deed. It involves lhe denial of self (Luke ix. 23). (2) It is the repudiation of ungodliness in heart and life. (a) Ungodliness includes impiety, blasphemy, and infidelity. (b) It includes all living without relation t.o God, whether we are blasphemers or not. Thus a man may be ungodly who seeks bis own pleasure, or distinction, or happiness in the world. (c) It implies the deeper enmity of the heart to God (Rom. viii. 7). (3) It is the donial of worldly lusts; including the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and vain glory of life-" all that is in the world "-which embody the enmity to God. Thus it denies (a) sensual lusts (2 Tim. ii. 22); (b) the inordinate d-re of worldly things, which may be lawful in themselves. 3. The grace of God produces certain positive effects. "We should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this prewnt world." (1) It secures the due regulation of individual life. "Soberly." This refers to the duties we owe t.o ourselves. (a) Jn keeping a fair balance of judgment intellectually; (b) in keeping a due mastery over our passions-" a sobriety in Apeech, in behaviour, in apparel, in eating and drinking, in recreations, and in the enjoyment of lawful satisfactions. (2) It secure~ the faithful discharge of o.11 duties to our fellow-men. "Righteously." Justice is an exact virtue, which can be easily measured, and is therefore the basis of commercial and civil life. A single failure in justice makeR a man unjust. Therefore it is most necessary we should give our neighbour his due, and not compromise ourselvea by TITUS. D THE h:l'l8TLE TO TITUS. (cu. 11. 1-15. conduct redounding to the injury of the gospel. (3) It secures godliness. "Godly•" t.hat is, with God, in God, for God. This godly life is a life dedicated t.o God and spe~t in his fear. III. THE SPHERE IN WHICH THIS GRACE or Goo PROIIU0E8 IT8 F.XTENBIVE AND INTENSIVE EFFECTS. "In this present world." 1. True piety does not disrfgard or despise the d1tties of common life. 2. It is in a hostile world this grace is to operate with smh p1trffying results. It is c:ctlled "this wickP<l world" (Gal. i. 4); for the devil is its god, Hud sin is its prevailing character. 3. It is a world that cannot be overcome but by.faith. (I John iv. 4, 5.) !. It is a transitory world, in conti-ast with the world to ooTM, of which the apostle immediatel.1· speaks. IV. THE ATTITUDE OF THE BELIEVER IN RELATION TO THE FUTURE GLORY, "Looking for the blessed hope and manifestation of our crreat God and Saviour Jesns Christ." This attitude of blessed expectation tells pow:;·fully 11pon the life of j!race. The believi,r's position is that of waiting for aud looking unto the corning of the Lord. ThP patriarchs waited for his first coming; we wait for his second coming. 1. The believer's waiting attitude is lit up by a blessed hope. (1) This is "the hope of glory" laid up for us in heaven, which is associated with the Son of God, when we shall see him as be is. (2) It is a blessed hope, because of all the blessings it brings to the bPliever. 2. The believer's waiting attitude has respect to the manifestation of the Lord'., glory. (3) The immerliate context applies only to the Son. (4) The term" great God" would seem to be uncalled for as applied to the Father, but stands in Scripture the perpetual and emµhatic witness of the Deity of Christ.-T. C.

entries.title: TIT 2:1–10
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -Genuine morality. "But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine," etc. Paul, having given Titus directions as to the organization of a Christian Church in Crete, and charged him to conten,l against those who, in the name of Christianity, propagated doctrines at variance both with the truths and the spirit of the gospel, here urges that genuine morality which should be the grand aim and tendency of all gospel preaching. The grand subject presented in this passage is genuine morality. '!'here have been, and still are, those who regard morality and religion as two distinct subjects or lines of conduct. But they are essentially one; one cannot exist without the other. The essence o( both consists in supreme regard to the Divine will as the only standard of character and rule of life. Frum these verses we may draw three general truths in relation to this subject. I. GENUINE MORALl'fY LEGISLATES ALIKE FOR ALL MANKIND. It speaks to man authoritatively, whatever his personal peculiarities, adventitious distinctions, social relations, secular circumstances, official position, the number of his years, or the characteristics of his country. Moral law meets him everywhere; he can no more escape it than he can the atmosphere he breathes. In these word~ persons are mentioned distinguished by three fundamental facts. 1. The/act of age. Amongst the millions of the race, not many in any geueration can be found that came into existence exactly at the same minute. Hence there are those differing in age from one year to a hundred or more. Hence Paul speaks here of" aged men" and" aged women,"" yuu11g men" and "young women." At the first dawn of moral consciousness, up to the last breath of earthly existence, the voice of duty sveaks-" Thus saith the Lord." No one bas strength enough to extricate himself from the ties of moral obligation. Not even that mighty spirit who leads the "world captive at his will" can break the shackles of moral responsibility. 2. The fact ef sex. Here are" men" and "women," both the aged and the young. However closely identified in affection and interest, moral duty treats each 118 a distinct- persouality. In human legislation the obligation of the woman, in some cases, is absorbed in that of the man. Not so with the moral legislation of Heaven. Ea.eh must bear its own burden, Inasmuch as the woman is as bound to follow the will of God as the man, no man has a right to interfere with the freedom of her thought, the dictates of her conscience, or the independency of her devotions. For long ages men have not recognized this fact, and they have treated women as their toys of pleasure and iI!strurnents of gratification. Women are beginning to wake up to their rights, ancl the day of man's tyranny is drawing to a close. 3. The/act efrelationship. Paul says, "Exhort servants to he obedient unto.their own masters." Why the duty of servants should be here referred to and not that of masters, is not because masters have not their duty, but perhaps at this time in Crete there were slaves who were disloyal and rebellious, Whilst the duty of servants is here referred to, the fact must not be overlooked that morality is binding on men in every social relationship, on the rulers as well aa the ruled, the judges as well as the criminals, the parents as well as the children, the employers as well as the employes. What is wrong for one is wrong for all, and the reverse, II. GENUINE MORALITY ~EACIIES TO THE SPRINGS OF THE HEART. It does not concern itself with the external conduct. " Bodily exercise profiteth but little." But as it regards external conduct as the evolutions of the states of the heart, it legislates ror those states. It says, "Keep the heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life." Glance at the virtues here inculcated. "That the aged men be sober [sober-minded], grave, temperate." The exhortation to sobriety is also addressed to aged women: "That they be not given to much wine." Also to the young women: "Teach the young women to be sober." And to the young men: "Exhort to be sober-minded." Although physica.l sobriety is undoubtedly referred to, mural sobriety, serious thoughtfulness, and selfrestraint are evidently included and regarded ns fanrlamental. Moral sober-mindedness is the effective preventative and cure of all physical intemperance. No argument, either for total nbstinence or against it, can be sustained by the phrase," Not give11 to much wine." All the words convey is-Do not get drunk. "Sound in fai~h, in charity [love], in patience." This means-Have a healthy faith, a faith well founded; a healthy love. «) THE EPISTLE 'l'O TITUB. [GB. u. 1-16. a love wtened on the supremely lovable; a healthy patience, a patience that ■ball bear up with fortitude and magnanimity under all the trials of life. 11 As becometh holiness "-reverent in demeanour. Let the whole life he full of that "holiness without which no man can Ill! the Lord." "Not false accusers"-not slanderers, It bas been observed that old women are specially tempted to garrulity and querulousness; hence the exhortation here. "Teachers ol' good things "--of that which is good. 'l'hings good in themaelves as well as in their tendencies and is5ues; teachers, not merely by words; but by example. "That they may teach [train] the young women t.o be sober." The expression, "to be sober," should be omitted. "To love their husbands." The duty implies that the husband is lol'eworthy; there are some men who are called husbands so morally abhorrent and disgusting, that t.o love them would be impossible. The ideal husband mUBt be loved. "To love their children." A mother's love, of a certain kind, is proverbial. M:ikrnal love, wrongly directed, has been one of the chief curses of thti race. "To be discreet "-sober-minded. A proper cheerfulness in mothers ~s a precious virtue, but volatile frivolousness is a serious evil. "Chaste "-purity of the body, fre&- dom from obscenity in language and life. Nothing in society is more beautiful then athoroughly chaste woman-chaste in language, chaste in dress, chaste in movement; and nothing is more disgusting then the reverse-a women unclean in appearance, in costume, in language, in manners. "Keepers [workers] et home." Wives must work as well as husbands. Work is a condition of health and of true enjoyment. An idle wife is a bane both to herself end her family. "At home." This may not mean entirely iu her own house, but in her own sphere, it may be in the garden, the (ield, the schoolroom., the Church, etc. "Good"-kind, amiable, sympathetic, generous, free from ell that is malign, envious, end jealous. "Obedient [being in subjection] to their own husbands." This implies, of course, that the husband's commauds ere wise, right, end useful. "That the Word of God be not blasphemed." This refers, perhaps, t.o ell the previous exhortations, end expresses a grand reason for the cultivation of ell virtues. Our conduct in ell thingil should be such e.s t.o bring honour rather than dishonour on our Lord end Master. "Let your light also so shine before men, that they may see your good works, end glorify your Father which is in heaven." "Young men likewise exhort t.o be sober-minded." Youth, in the swelling streams of its passions, the wild play of it.s fancy, end its craving for the romantic, is fearfully exposed to mental insobriety. Hence, no duty for the young is more urgent than that of obtaining a selfmasterhood. Titus, whom Paul commends to exhort young men t.o this duty, was himself a comparatively young man. He could scarcely have been more than forty, years of age. "Brought up in a pagan home, 11ot improbably in the ln.xurioUB end wicked Syrian Antioch, drawn to the Master's side in the fresh dawn of manhood, tried in many a difficult t.ask end found faithful, the words of Titus exhorting the youth of Crete to be sober-minded or self-restrained would be likely to have greet weight." "In ell things showing thyself a pattern [ensemple] of good works, in doctrine showing uncorrnptnes:;, gravity, sincerity,sound speech that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary pa.rt may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you rus]." In order that the exhortations of Titus might he\·e full force, Paul here edaresses an admonition to him. He is to show himself a "pattern of good works" in ell things; he is to be a model of excellence in ell his relation~ to the men end women of Crete, both the aged and the young. He IllUBt be pure, grave, and sincere. His preaching, too, should he such that could not be "condemned "-sound, healthy, practical, not fanciful, sentimental, and morbid. Ah I how many sermons preached every Sunday men of reason, thoughtfulness, conscience, recoil from and condemn I "Exhort se"ents to be obedient [in subjection] to their own masters, end to please them well [to be well plea.sing to them] in ell things; not answeri11g agaiu [not gainsaying]; not purloining, but showing ell good fidelity." Herein is enjoined on servants obedience, acquiescence, honesty, faithfulness. All this implies, of course, that the master is what he ought to be, that hie commends ere righteous, that his words ere truthful, and that the work he enjoins is lawful end right. "That they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in ell things." From this it would seem that even sieves, in righteously serving their masters, may even honour God in their humble service. Thus from thls passage we learn that genuine morality reaches the very springs of the heart, the fountain of ell ....:tiona. He ill not a morel men who only acts in strictest conformity to the oonnn- OIL D. 1-16,] THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. tione.l rules of society, nor 111 be enn e. moral man who merely fulfils the letter of the Divine commands. "All these commandments he.ve I kept from my youth up.... Yet one thing thou le.ckest," etc. He only is the true me.n whose governin(7 sympathies flow in the channels of eterne.l right, and whose activities are ever engaged ~ endeavours t-0 please the mighty Me.ker of his being. The will of God, and that only, is the datum of true ethics. III. GENUINE MODALITY 18 THE GRAND PURPOSE OIi' GOSPEL TEACHING. "But speak thou the things which become [befit] sound doctrine, that the aged men," etc. His tee.ching is to be in contrast with that of the false teachers mentioned in the previou, verses, and which led to immorality of conduct. This verse and the seve11th, urging Titus, as a preacher, to be a pattern in all things, both in his teaching and his cnn<luct, justifies the inference that the grand end of gospel teaching is the promotion of genuine 'TTWT'ality. In the eighth verse of the next chapter, Paul distinctly states that Titus WB8 so to teach that his hearers might be "careful to maintain good works." This is a point which what is called the "Church" hBS, in its teachings, practically ignored. The gospel has been preached to sustain theologies, to establish sects, and to maintai11 certain institutions, ecclesiastical and political, instead of rnakiDg men 'TTWT'ally good, honesr, faithful, e.nd heroically loyal to the "truth as it is in Jesus." Here, then, we have the only infallible tat ofpulpit usefulnes,. In what does the real utility of the pulpit consist? In gathering large audiences? Any charlatan can do this; and, frequently, the greater the charlatan the most successful. In generating in the congregation the largest amount of superficial religious sentiment? This often emasculates the reason, diseases the conscience, enervates the will, and renderf the whole atmosphere of the soul insalubrious and depressing. No; but in making men 'TTWT'al, the living agents evermore of good works. I estimate a true Church, not by the number of its members, the apparent earnestness of its devotions, or the amount of its contributions, but by the number of its professors who are too truthful to lie, too honest to defraud, too morally noble to do or to countenance a mean or a dishonourable act-to whom, in short, e.11 worldly wealth and power, and life itself, are held cheap as dirt compe.red with the right. When Churches are made up of such members, then, and not until then, they will command tbe confidence, the sympathy, the trade, and the influence of the world. Well does Emerson say, " There is no morality without religion, and there is no religion without morality. •This is the love of God, the.t we keep his commandments.' He who loves God keeps the commandment, loves God in action. Love is obedience in the heart, obedience is love in the life. Morality is religion in practice, religion is morality in principle."-D. T.

entries.content: -'l'he ,oul...cullure of thtJ world. "For the grace of God that bringeth salvation bath appeared to all men," etc. "Taking occasion from what he had just said of the connection between the conduct of Christians and the doctrine they professed to have received, and the connection of both with the glory of God, the apostle proceeds in these ver&es to ground the whole of his exhortations respecting tb,i behaviour of Christians in the essentially moral nature and design of the graclil of God, as now manifested in the gospel" (Dr. Fairbairn). As if the apostle had said, " You must exhort all orders, those of every age and condition, of each sex, bond as well as free, to struggle after spiritual goodness because the •grace of God,' or the gospel, has come to you." Our subject is the soul-culture of thtJ world. Man requires training. He needs physical training, intellectual training, and, above all, spiritual training, the tre.ining of the soul into a higher life. We have here the instrument, the process, and the md of true soul-culture. I. TBE IM8TBUME!o"'J OJI' TBUE SOUL-OULTtrRE. What is it? Not science, legisla- •tion, philosephy, poet,y, or any of the arts. What, then? "'!'he grace of God." Whe.t is that? Undoubtedly God's merciful plan and ministries to restore the fallen world. The Epiphany, or manifestation of this redemptive love of God for the world, we he.ve in the advent and ministry of Christ to this earth. "The grace of God" stands for the gospel. Concerning this instrument, observe : 1. It is the l011e of God. Divine love ie the cause, tht' essence, and the efi"ootive energy of all God'~ redemptive ministries. 2. II ia the love of God to ,aw. "That bringeth [bringing] salvation." Salvation, that is, the restoration of me.n to the knowledge, the imege, and the frit1ncl- 42 THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. [ou. n. 1-16, ship of God. This is the aim and the work of the "grace of God." Without this \!rRCe there woulrl be no salvation. 3. It is tM love of God revealed to all. "Hnth appeared to all men." The gospel is not for a tribe or a clas8, but for man as man, Like the co11c1\\'e f,..1\l'ens, it embraces the wide world; it is for "all men." II. THE rRocF.ss OF TRUE SOUL-CULTURE. 'l'his process involves three things. L. The re1mnc,:11tion of a wrong course. "Denying ungodliness and worldly lusts," These expn•ssious are an epitome of all that is sinful and wrong in human lile. Aro they not all-pre,·alent and all-potent? "Ungodliness," or practical atheism, where is ,t not? "Worldly lusts," the imp_ulses of sensuality, selfishness, pride, a11d ambition, they are the springs of worldly action the world over. Now, these are not only to be renou11ced, repudiated, but they are to be defied, resisten, and renounced; they must be given up. " U11,_:odlim·ss" must give way to true piety, "worldly lusts" must be renounced for impulses spiritual and Divine. 2. The adoption of a right course. "We should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world." It is net enough to renounce the evil; tl:e good must be adopted. Negative excellence ia not holiness. S1 rip the soul of a.II evil, and if it has not "Oodness in it, it "lacks the one thing" without which, Paul says, "I am nothing." We must live "soberly,n holding " mastery over our own passions and impulses; "righteously," re1,dering to all men their due; "12:od ly," practically realizing the presence, the claims, and the love of God in our e\'ery-day life. All this" in this present world," or in the present course of tl1ings. This " present world" urgently requires such a course of life, for it is danc:erous and transitory withal. 3. The .fizing of tM heart upon a glorious future. ·• Looking for that blessed hope and the glorious appearance of the [appearing of the glory of our] '.!reat God and our Saviour Jesus Christ." Are there two personalities liere, or one'? 011e, 1 think. "The great God our Saviour," or our great God and Saviour. The object of hope is, then, the future epiphany of the Divine, all glorious to behold. To see the redemptive God as we have never yet seen him in this morally hazy scene, this is the "blessed hope." Such a hope implies: (1) A vital interest in the epiphany. We never hope for that for which we have not a strong desire. (~) An assura11ce that such an epiphany will take place. Desire, of itself, is not hope. We desire many things we cannot hope for. It becomes hope when it is combined with expectation, and expectation implies the existence of grounds or reasons. That there will be such a manifestation, there a.re abundant reasons found in the "PP"rent irregularities of Divine Providence in its operations here, in the instinctivto longings of the human soul throughout all lands and ages, as well as in the clear and frequent declaration~ of the written Word. IIL THE END OF TRUE souL-01,LTURE. "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniqui1y, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works." Observe: 1. The end is moral redemption. "Redeem us frorn all iniquity."' Redemption is not something that takes place outside of a man; its achievement is within. It is a raising of the soul from ignorance to knowledge, from vice to virtue, fron, selfishness to disinterestedness, from materialism to spirituality, from the mastery ul the devil to the reign of God. 2. The end is spiritual re.~toration to Chri.~t. "Purify unto himself a peculiar people [a people for his own possession]." Restoration to his likeness, his friendship, his service. 3. entries.title: TIT 3:1–7
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -Mercy liegetting mercy. The practical lessons or tbe gospel were not exha11sted in the preceding chapter, nor the motives which urge believers to godliness. Th<' call to holiness in the last chapter was based upon the holy character of God's saving grace and the purpose of Christ's redeeming love. In these verses the grace and love of God are still the basis of the exhortation, but it takes its peculiar colourinii; from the thought of what we were ourselves. Tenclerness, indulgence, and meeknes8 toward our fellow-men are the duties to which these verses call us; and it is supposed that those fellow-men may be rouii;b and evil-minded toward us, and provoking in their ways, and perhaps obstinate in evil-doing. The natural heart might be ready to speak evil of them, to contend fiercely with them, utterly to reject them as reprobates, to thrust them beyond the pale of hope and kindness. But stay! What were you yourselves when the kindness and love of God first appeared unto you? Were you walking in righteousness? Were your works the things which attracted God's love toward you? Nay I you were living in that folly which you now condemn in others; you were children of disobedience then as truly as they are now; you were deceived by sin then as they are now; you were the siaves of your own lusts then even as they are now ; you lived in malice and envy then, both hateful and hating one another. But God's mercy found you out; God's love threw a veil over your sins; he provided a fountain to wash away your guilt; he sent his Holy Spirit to create in you a clean heart, and to renew a right spirit within you; he justified you by his grace; he made you his heirs, and gave you the hope of eternal life. And will not you have mercy upon your fellow-men? Will not you, for whom the Divine gentleness and patience has done so much, be gentle and patient too? Will not you, bumble in the remembrance of yonr own sins, and abashed at the thought of your own unworthiness, deal meekly and kindly even with unruly and sinful men, and cherish the hope that God's boundless grace may at last reach them, even as it reached you? Thus the doctrine of God's mercy towarrl men begets mercy from man to man, and the doctrine of grace is the strongest conceivable motive to charity.

entries.title: TIT 3:8–15
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -Pearls before swine. There is in some a habit of mind utterly out of harmony with the Word of God. It is not that dogmas, or creeds, or ceremonies are despised anrl forgotten by them, as they usually are by the pleasure-seeking or moneymaking world. On the contrary, these things are often in their minds anrl upon their lips. But they hanrlle everything, not with a view to growth in goodness, not with a view to the formation within of a humble, pure, and holy character, but merely as matters of disputation. They raise questions, the solution of which has no bearing upon our duty to God or man, but which only give ocrasion for strife of worrls, and utterly unprofitable contentions. The most solemn truths, the most sacred mysteries of the Christian faith, are only food for a wrangling, disputatious spirit. They are always ready to start difficulties, to suggest doubts, or to propose new form■ of doctrintt 48 THE EPISTLE TO TITUS, [oe. m. 1-16, in lieu of thoee onoe delivered to the saints. Strong in their own conceit& and wise in thelr own esteem, they will not leam, no, not from Christ himself, hut are alwayd forward to teach some new thing. They value nothing which they have not invented themselves. They aooept no truth which they have not adulterated with their own imii.gine.tions. Disciples they will not be. Masters they must be. When this habit of mind has clearly developed itself, the serve.nt of God he.s only to withdraw from s1;1ch. He must not be drawn into the whirlpool of vain je.ngling and unprofite.ble disput.es. He must not go on casting his ll8&1'ls before the swine. Silence is, in such cases, the best rebuke. When honest e.nd gentle efforts to bring home to such persons the truths of God's Word in e. reverential and practical way have utterly failed, e.nd it is become evident the.t there is no desire in their hearts for Christ and his Word, it is time to cease from such efforts. "From such tum awe.y" is the authoritative advice of St. Paul. Nothing can be in sharper contrast with the "unprofitable strivings" here condemned than the unobtrusive works of kindness, and active help to the furtherance of the gospel, inculcated upon Titus. Zenas and Apollos are to be brought on their way. Care is to be taken that they want for nothing. The Church in Crete is to be fruitful in good works for the wants of their brethren ; and even the closing salutation is redolent of love and kindness. When Christians feel that the very essence of Christianity is unobtrusive love and kindness, shown in unselfish acts, and e. ree.d.iness to help wherever help is needed, then will the Church be Christ's true witness upon earth; witnessing to Christ e.s the embodiment of the law of love, and witnessing to the Spirit of Christ as dwelling in her of a truth.

entries.title: TIT 3:1
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -Political duties. The apostle now turns to the duties which Christians owe to the pagan world around them. L THE !o'ECESSITY OF THE INJUNCTION TO POLITICAL SUBMISSION. "Put them in mind." The words imply that the duty was already known, but needed to be recalled to Cretan memory. It is but too certain that the injunction was needed. Once a democratic state, now for over e. century under Roman Jaw, and always remarkable for a factious e.nd turbulent spirit, the Crete.n impatience of authority was reinforced by the spirit of insuhordine.tion which was such a characteristic of the Jewish part of the community. II. THE DUTY OF SUBMISSION TO CONSTITUTED AUTHORITY. "Put them in mind to be subject to e.uthorities, to powers, to obey the magistrate, to be ready towards every good work." The very redundancy of words used here is eignificant, as if to exclude the possibility of an eve.sion of the comme.nd. 1. Gover'f'.,ment is of God. "The powers that be are ordaintld of God" (Rom. xiii. 1; 1 Pet. iL 13). 2. Theform ofgovernment does not affect the duty of obed:ience. Monarchies, republics, oligarchies, have in them alike the ordination and power of God for the welfare of society. 3. There are limits to thiB obedience, but the apostle does not fiz them. The exceptional cases are not mentioned, because they a.re summed up either in ihe primary Je.w of self-preservation, which is antecedent to e.ll government, or in the supremacy of conscience, which must e.lways obey God rather than men. A king may become insane and murder his subjects, but the first principles of nature justify their resort to force in self-protection (Acts v. 29; iv. 9, 20). The king may command his subjects to practise idole.try. In that ca11e, if the Christian cannot resist, he must die. ill POLITICAL DUTY IN THE CABE OF CHRISTIANS INCLUDES MORE THAN SUBMISSION. They must be "ready toward every good work." As the magistre.tc is appointed to be a terror to evil-doers and the praise of them that do well (Rom. xiii. 3), the disposition of Christian subjects to every good work has a tendency to make government ee.ay and light.-T. entries.title: TIT 3:3
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -.An humiliating retrospect. The apostle adds, as a reason for the duties first specified, that "we also," including himself with the Gentile Christians, were once in a similar condition to the heathen, and had received mercy. It is a dark picture of men in their natural state, proceeding from a description of the inward source to the outwarrl racts of this evil Ufe. • I. HUllAN NATURE DEPl<YrED AB TO ITS MORE INWARD CBARAOTER. "For we ourselves" were once foolish. 1. It isfoolish. As wisdom is the choice of proper means of attaining our ends, so folly must be the direct contrary. (1) The fool despises instruction and wisdom, ancl hates knowledge (Prov. i. 7, 22). (2) He walks in the darkness of a false education (Eccles. ii. 14). (3) He is self-sufficient and self-confident (Prov. xiv. 8, 16). (4) He is a self-deceiver (Prov. xiv. 8). (5) He makes a mock at sin (Prov. xiv. 9). 2. It ia disobedient. The word implies that the root of all true obedience is faith. Human nature is without faith, and is therefore disobedient. (1) Disobeclience forfeits God's favour (1 Sam. xiii. 14). (2) Provokes his anger (Ps. lxxviii. 10, 40). (3) Forfeits promised blessings (Josh. v. 6). (4) Brings a curse (Deut. xi. 28). (6) There are many warnings against it (Jer. xii. 17). 3. It is deceived. Because it is separated from Christ, who is the Light of the world. It is easily led astray by all sorts of delusion. It has no pole-star or compass to steer by, and is therefore in constant danger of shipwreck. It is deceived by it.self as well as by the devil. II. This was the character of heathen life in an island like Crete, where the propensities of human nature would have free scope. The pleasures of this life were of a sinlul and debasing nature. Such a service was bondage (Rom. vi. 6, 16; xvi. l8). 2. It implied a life of malice. (1) The wicked speak with malice (3 John 10). (2) Are filled with it (Rom. i. 29). (3) Visit the saints with it (Ps. lxxxiii. 3). (4) God requites it (Isa. x. 14). 3. it implied a life of envy. (1) Envy is a work "f the flesh (Gal. v. 21). (2) The wicked are full of it (Rom. i. 29). (3) It leads to everv evil work (Jae. iii. 16). (4) It is hurtful to its possessors (Job v. 2). (5) It will be punished (Ps. cvi. 16, 17). 4. It implies hatefulness. "Hateful;" that is, possessing the qualities that excite hatred and dislike. 5. It implies a return of hale for hate. "Hating one another." (1) It is characteristic of those without love to God (1 John ii. 9, 11). (2) It is a work of the flesh (Gal. v. 21). (3) It stirs up strife (Prov. x. 12). (4) It embitters life (Prov. xv. 17). (6) It will be punished (Ps. xxxiv. 21).-T. C.

entries.title: TIT 3:4–7
entries.author: Arthur Charles Hervey
entries.content: -T/ie origin, nature, means, anrl end of salvation. The iipostle re_flects that he and other believers had no excuse for treating the heathen with baught1ness, since it was owin" to no merit of his or theirs that their own lives had become purer. I. THE MANIF;BTATION OF THE DIVINE GOODNESS AND LOVJI TO MA.N. "But when the kindness of God our Saviour and his l0Vt1 to man appearecl." 1. The time of lhie Tl'l'UH. • 50 THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. [OB. ID, 1-16, manifest,atwn. The expression implies a definite point of time. It was" the fulness of the time" (Gal. iv. 4). (1) It Willi tho period fixed in the Divine purpose from eternity. (2) lt was the time of the probation of the Jews, ending in the most awful series of judgments that ever befell a people. (3) It was a time when the Oreek tongne and the Roman arms made a highway for the gospel. (4) It was a time when pauan thought bad exhausted every experiment in the art of living, to find that all ;as "vanity and "exation of spirit." (5) Yet it is not impliPd that the manifestation of Divine kindness had not been enjoyed already in pre-Christia11 ages; for it was in virtue of this manifestation, in the fulness of times, that God's love flowed forth in blessing during Jewish ages. 2. The nature of thi,s manifestatioo. (1) It was a manifestation of kindness and love to mau. (a) Kindness is the more genera.I term, unlimited, undefined, all-embracing, touching the whole creation. (b) Love to man is his special and distinguishing love to the children of men as distinct from angels. (2) It was the love of the Father-" our Saviour-God." (a) The title" Saviour," ~o often given to the don, is here given to the Father, because he is the Fountain from whence flow a.II the streams of Di,·ine mercy. The Son is" the Unspeakable of the Father;" for he "so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son" (John iii. 16). The atonement was not, therefore, the cause, but the effect, of the Father's love. (b) This fact, exhibiting the mine of power and love in the Crea.tor, greatly enhances the certainty and glory of redemption. (c) It is our Father who is our Saviour. Mark the clear relationship, in spite of all our wa)·wardness and siu. II. 'l'HE METHOD OF THIS DIVINE MAND'ESTATlON. "Not by works of righteousness we did, but according to his mercy he saved us." The Divine g00dness and love were manifested in salvation. "He saved us." This salvation, procured hy the obedience and death of Christ, has its origin, not in works of righteousness done by man, as ,•ntitlin2 him to it, but solely in Divine mercy. Mark the conditions and the means .,f this salvation. 1. The conditions efsalvation. (1) Not by works of righteousness. (a) "'e are Dot saved by our own works, even though thl'Y should be done in obedience to a rigb1eous law (Rom. iii. 20; Gal. ii. 16; Epb. ii. 4, 8, 1:1; 2 Tim. i. 1, 9). (b) If we were saved in this way, Christ should have died in vain (Gal. ii. 21). His death would have been quite unneceBS&ry. (c) Experience proves the impossibility of our heing able to do the works of perfect righteousness (Rom. iii. 23). (2) The condition .,f salvation is Divioe mercy. "According to bis mercy." (a) God is rich in mercy (Eph. ii. 4). (b) It streams forth from the blood and righteousness of Christ (Rom. iii. 24, 25; vi. 23). (c) It was through the tender mercy of God that Christ, as the Dayspring from on high. visited the earth (Luke i. 78). (d) The pardon of sin is according to the multitude of bis tender mercies (Ps. li. 1, 2). (e) Eternal life is the effect of God's mercy. 2. The meanB of salvatwn. "By the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Ghost, which he poured on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour." The Greek word is" !aver," as if to show that the reference is to haptism.. (1) The washing of re.generation refers to the beginning of .the spiritual process in the sonl, as it is the Spirit who regenerates the soul. There is nothing in the passage to support the doctrine of baptismal regeneration. (a) The connection of baptism with regeneration no more proves that all the baptized are regenerated than the expression, "we are sanctified by the truth," implieF that the truth in all cases has this effect, or that "the gospel of your salvation" implies that salvation always follows the hearing of the gospel (b) As a matter of fact, believers in apostolic times were regenerated before they were baptized ; therefore they were not regenerated by bapti9m. This was the case with the three thousand at Pentecost (Acts ii.), with Lydia and the Philippian ja.ilor (Acts xvi.). (c) There is no necessary connection between baptism and regeneration, for Simon Magus was baptized without being regenerated (Acts viii. 9-24). (d) It is strange that, much a..s John speaks of regeneration in his First Epistle, he never connoots baptism with it. He says that those who ue "born of God" do righteousness, and overcome the world. Why should he mention r.aeae teats at all, when he might have known that, had they been baptized, they must t•MVA been reuenerated? (e) The Apostle Peter shows us the meaning of bapti11-m when 1;:;: aays that~. baptism doth now save us" (1 Pet, iii. 21). How? "Not by putting ll.way· the filth of the flesh "-which is ea.Hily clone bv the external application of water -~ but the answer ufa good conscie::icP- toward Go~·· ae if to show that such an answer, CB, DI, 1-16.] THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. 51 representing the reality and sincerity of our profession, was separable from the putting away of the filth of the flesh. (./) The expression, "baptism for the remission of sins," does not imply that baptism is the cause of their remi.•sion, for in all the cases referred to the remission bad already taken place before baptism (Acts ii. 38; xxii. 16). The baptism was a sign or seal of a remission already accomplished. Saul was a true believer before Ananias said to him, "Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the Name of the Lord." BcHides, it was by calling on the Name of the Lord that his sins were washed away. Tltis is the force of the Greek construction. (2) The renewing of the Holy Ghost refers to the continuancP. of the spiritual process in the soul. ThuR "the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor. iv. 16). This points to progreRsive sanctification. (a) The renewed are the cbilrlren of God, tht' heirs of the eternal inheritance. (b) The effects are the fruits of righteousne.~s in our life and conversation. Thus there is a firm connection between the regeneration and the renewal, which cannot be said of baptism and renewal. Christendom is baptized, y, t how little grace is manifest among its millions! (c) The source of this renewal is the Holy Ghost, who has been poured out upon us richly through Jesus Christ our Saviour. It was in virtue of the mediatorship that the Spirit was given, and still works in the Church of God. For (11) all salvation is by him; (fJ) the grace of regeneration is out of his fulness; (-y) the gift of God, which is eternal life, is through him. III. THE END OF THIS MANIFESTATION OF DIVINE GOODNESS AND LOVE. .. That beini;: justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life." God saves us according to his mercy by regeneration ; but the first effect of regeneration is faith, and faith is the instrument of our justification. There is no difference in the order of time between regeneration and justification, but regeneration must precede justification in the order of nature. Therefore the apostle here goes upon the order of nature. 1. The nature ofJ°t,stification. It inclurles pardon of sin and acceptance into God's favour. 2. The ground ofjustification. "Being justified by his grace." (1) Not by wCJrks; (2) but by the grace of the Father, who is the Justifier. It is hy grace. because (a) it is of faith (Rom. v, 1; iii. 28); (b) it is by the <leath of the Son of God. 3. The privileges of justification. "That we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life." (1) l•:ternal life is an inheritance; it is not earned by our obedience and our righteousness; it is a free gift. (2) We are predestinated to this inheritance in Jesus Christ (Eph. i. 5, 11). (3) The grace of adoption, which is linked with our justification, opens the way to our enjoyment of the inheritance. (4) It is an inheritance which is not yet fully enjoyed; for we are heirs "accoruing to the hope of eternal life." (a) There are '' things hoped for" held out to us through faith (Heh. xi. 1). (b) "It doth not yet appear what we shall be;" but when "we shall be for ever with the Lord," we shall actually possess and enjoy our inheritance.-T. C.

entries.title: TIT 3:8

entries.content: -The necessary connection betweffl gospel doctrine and good works. I. THE IMPORTAN0E OF GOSPEL DOCTRINE. "This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm consta11tly." He refers here to the sum nf the doctrl11e of Christian salvation contained in the three preceding verses. 1. The doctrine of salvation is worthy ofall acceptance. "This is a faithful saying." This formula, contained only in the pastoral Epistles, points to some weighty truth which had become a watchword among the Christian brotherhood of early times. (1) There is a tendency in our days to decry dogma. 'l'he apostle always insists on its importance as the root-principle and moving spring of morality. (2) The saying implies that the heavenly inheritance just spoken of is no figment of the imagination, hut ought to be accepted as one of the commonplaces of Christian belief. 2. Jt ought eo be crmfidenely put forth at all times by Ohriseian ministers. " And these things I will that thou affirm constantly." This was the strain of a.II apostolic preachiug, and it ought to be ours al~n. There is no true practical preaching which does not involve the exhibition of God's character and our relations to him in grace-the glorious Person of the Mediator in his various offices, and the work of the Holy Ghost in appl_ving Divine salvation. "These things art> good and profitable to men ; " that is, these doctrines, for they lead to good works, and be11efit men spiritually and morally. II. THE DESIGN OF GOSPEL DOCTIUNE. "In order that they which have believed God might be careful to maintain good works." The faithful saying of the apostle was not 52 THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. These are, therefore probably called doctrines according to godliness (eh. i. 1); the wholesome doctrin~ (eh. i. 9). 2. He sets forth tM duty of all believers to be careful about good works. lt ought to be a matter of earnest striving, because (1) God is glorified thereby (Jo)rn xv. 8); (2) because 1he.1· a.re means of blessing to man (Jas. i. 26); (3) because God remembers them (Heb. vi. 9, 10); (4) because they will be an evidence of faith in the judgment (Matt. xxv. 34-40). 3. (1) They must, therefore, be zealous of 1hem (eh. ii. 14); (2) furnished unto them (2 Tim. iii. 17); (3) rich in them, and ~tablished in them (1 Tim. vi. 18; 2 Thess. ii. 17); (4) ready for all good works (eh. iii. 1); (5) provoking each other unto them (Heb. x. 24).-T. C.

entries.content: -.A warning against frivolo1llJ and di.~putative teaching. This is in contrast to the sound teaching just referred to. "But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contention~, and strivings about the Law; for they are unprofitable and vain." l. THE THINGS WHICH ARE TO BE PLACED OUTSIDE THE SPHERE OF MINISTERIAL THOUGHT AND coNcrnN. 1. Ji'ooli.sh qu,e,stions. Questions not easily answererl, yet i( answered without practical bearing upon Christian life. Such were many of the Jewish discussions about the oral Law, the nature of God and the angels, the power of the Name Jehovah. Contentions and strivings about the Law. There were many disputed and disputable points in the Law, especially respecting the authority and confirmation of the commandments (eh. i. 14). II. THE A'l"l'ITUDE OF THE :MINISTER TOWARD SUCH THINGS. "Avoid them." 1. This implia that he i6 not even to di.scuss them, on account of their utter frivolousness. 2. The reason is that they are "unprofitable and vain," and therefore exactly opposed to the things "good and profitable to men." The apostle would deliver all ministers from such folly and trifling, by placing before them Jesus Christ, the one glorious Object of the Church's Jove and adoration, leaving questions of another sort to the dead. Such questions had eaten the heart out of Judaism. They must not be allowed in Christianity.-T. C.

entries.title: TIT 3:10

entries.content: -The right attit?Uh of Christian minister, toward divisive errorirts. "A man that is an heretic after a first and second admonition avoid." L THE TBUE NATURE OF HIS OFFENCE. 1. entries.content: -The mercy of God. "According to hie mercy be l!llved us." Mercy is th_e _key-note of redemption. It is the music of the Psalms; the spirit of ChrisL's mrmstry, and the motive of the atonement. It is the very heart of God-as permanent as his justice and bis righteousness; "for bis mercy endureth for ever." I. SALVATION IS NOT A SUPERSTRUCTURE OF MAN'S. "Not according to works of righteousness which we have done." Good actions do not make a good man; it is the ~ood man that makes the good actions. If man is to be saved, he must have new life fron, within. Mercy meets his case. God's pity and compassion are seen in this. He gives the new heart that makes the new lire, and so he saves us from self and sin. II. SALVATION IS A DUAL WORK. This is" the washing of regeneration," the redemption that comes to the heart through the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness. But the removal or the stain of sin is not all. The heart, however clean, is not to be a blank. • A rww likeness is to be brought out. So there is to be the "renewing of the Holy Ghost." We are made new creatures in Christ Jesus. God's likeness comes out again in the soul. We are made holy with God's holiness, and beautiful with God'e beauty.-W. M. S.

entries.content: -Christian characfm'. "To maintain good works."
